title: Tracing a hydraulic circuit, then a pneumatic one

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the ram move as oil lights up from the pump into one side of the cylinder and from the other side to the tank, when you tap -Y1 or -Y2.
interactive.title: The press
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens. Some show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. The main picture is a press, drawn as a hydraulic circuit. At the bottom, motor -M1 drives a pump. The pump draws oil from the tank through a filter and feeds the valve's P port. A relief valve sits on the pump's line. It opens to the tank when the pressure beats its spring. A gauge beside it reads the pump's pressure. It has no numbers, only a mark at the relief valve's setting. Above is a 4/3 valve, drawn as a row of three boxes. Its fixed ports are P and T below, and A and B above. The left box joins P to A and B to T. The right box's crossed arrows join P to B and A to T. The middle box joins P to T and blocks A and B. Solenoid -Y1 and a spring sit at the left end. Solenoid -Y2 and a spring sit at the right. At the top the cylinder stands upright. Its rod points down to the ram. The work sits on a bed below. A goes to the piston side, at the top. B goes to the rod side, at the bottom. On the line from B, a flow control and a check valve sit side by side. Both join the same two points. The check valve lets oil pass only into the rod side. Each part has its name beside it. The rule. Each solenoid brings in the box beside it. That box sets two paths, one into the cylinder and one out. A line carrying flow is bold with arrows. An idle line is pale. With -Y1 on, oil runs from P to A into the piston side. Oil from the rod side runs through the flow control and B to T, to the tank. The ram comes down. The flow control lets the rod side's oil out slowly. So a fixed pump's spare oil goes over the relief valve, drawn as a thinner dashed line. When the ram meets the work, it stops. All the pump's oil then goes over the relief valve, and the needle sits on the relief mark. With -Y2 on, oil runs from P to B through the check valve into the rod side. Oil from the piston side runs through A to T, to the tank. The ram goes back up. At the top no more oil can get in. So the pump's oil goes over the relief valve. Tapping a solenoid switches it on and the other off. Tapping it again switches it off. With both off, the springs bring the middle box back. P to T is lit, the ram holds and the needle sits near zero. A Stop button stops the pump and switches both solenoids off. The gauge reads zero. A cylinder line whose oil still holds a load is then drawn red. Its label says "still under pressure". If the ram was pressing the work, that is the line from A. The middle box shut it in. If the ram hangs above the work, it is the line from B. Its oil holds up the ram's weight. The button then reads Start. Tap it to restart. A caption under the pump says what it is doing: feeding the cylinder, unloading to the tank, going over the relief valve, or stopped. Below the press is the air card. It does the same job in air. A compressor and its receiver feed a service unit. The service unit cleans the air and sets its pressure. Then comes a 5/2 valve, with solenoid -Y3 at one end and a spring at the other. Its two working lines go to a double-acting cylinder. Each exhaust port ends in an exhaust mark, with a small arrow into the room. At rest the spring holds the box that feeds the rod side and exhausts the piston side. So the rod stays in. Tap -Y3 and the supply fills the piston side. The rod side's air leaves through an exhaust port, and the rod comes out. Tap it again and the spring brings the rod back in. Beside it is a squeeze test. It has two small cylinders with their ports shut, one of air and one of oil. Each has a load on its rod. A load slider sets the pressure each load makes. It runs from 6 to 12 bar absolute, in steps of 1. At 6 the air fills 300 cm³. The air keeps pressure times volume the same. So a readout shows its volume as 1800 divided by the pressure, in cm³. At 12 the air fills 150 cm³, and its rod has gone in. The oil's rod does not visibly move. The lesson opens with the motor running and both solenoids off. The ram is held near the top, -Y3 is off and the slider is at 6. At phone width the solenoid buttons and Stop wrap onto two rows, with no word split. The air card sits below the press. Every label is at least 12 px and readable at 360 px. Screen by screen. Screen 1, do, typed, Still there?: a small cylinder with its ports shut, air inside and a load on its rod. "Air shut in a cylinder fills 300 cm³ at 6 bar absolute. A heavier load raises its pressure to 9 bar absolute, at the same temperature. What volume does the air fill now?" A typed answer: 200, in cm³, a whole number. Slips: 450, "That is the pressures upside down. More pressure squeezes the air smaller."; 300, "Air squeezes. Its volume falls as its pressure rises." Hint: "Pressure times volume stays the same." Why: pressure times volume stays at 6 × 300, which makes 1800. So the volume is 1800 ÷ 9, which is 200 cm³. The heavier load pushes the rod in. A right answer says "Still there." After Check, the press appears. Screen 2, show, The job first: the press as it opens. Words: "This is a press. Its ram comes down onto the work, squeezes it and goes back up. Read the job first. Then name the parts. Then trace one valve position at a time." The parts light in turn, each with its name. The gauge's needle sits near zero. Read: the press at rest, with every part named. Still: the end of the sweep. Screen 3, do, As drawn: the press as it opens. "The motor runs and no solenoid is energised. What does the ram do?" Choices: It holds, and the pump's oil goes back to the tank (right); It comes down onto the work; It holds, and the pump's oil goes over the relief valve. Hint on It comes down: "No solenoid is on, so the springs hold the middle box against the ports. Read that box." Hint on the relief valve: "Look at P in the middle box. Its line runs straight to T." Why: the sheet draws the valve at rest, with its middle box against the ports. That box joins P to T and blocks A and B. So the pump's oil goes back to the tank at low pressure, and the ram holds. After Check, the line from P to T lights. Screen 4, show, Two paths: the press as it opens. Words: "Energise -Y1 and the left box joins P to A and B to T. Oil from the pump fills the piston side. The rod side's oil runs back to the tank. The ram moves only if both paths are open, so follow both." Then "Tap -Y1." Read: -Y1 is on. Oil runs from P to A into the piston side. The rod side's oil runs through the flow control and B to T, to the tank. The ram comes down. Still: the ram half way down. Screen 5, do, The other side: -Y1 marked as on, the ram coming down, only the path into the piston side lit. "Tap the parts the rod side's oil passes on its way to the tank, in order." The answer: the flow control, then the valve, then the tank. Hint on the check valve: "The check valve lets oil pass only into the rod side. Going out, the oil must take the flow control." Hint on the pump: "The pump only feeds. Oil leaving the cylinder goes back to the tank." Hint otherwise: "Start at the rod side and follow its line down to B." Why: the check valve is shut this way, so the rod side's oil leaves through the flow control. The left box joins B to T, so the oil runs back to the tank. Without that path the ram could barely move. After Check, the path lights. Screen 6, show, On the work: -Y1 on, the ram half way down. Words: "The flow control lets the rod side's oil out slowly, so it sets the ram's speed. This pump pushes out the same amount every turn. The slowed cylinder takes less, so the pressure rises until the relief valve opens. The spare oil goes over it. So the relief valve's setting decides how hard the ram presses." Then "Watch the ram meet the work." Read: the ram has stopped on the work. The pump's oil runs over the relief valve to the tank, and the needle sits on the relief mark. Still: the ram on the work. Screen 7, do, What sets the squeeze?: the ram on the work, -Y1 still on, no path lit and no caption. "The ram is pressing the work and -Y1 is still on. Which part decides how hard it presses?" Choices: The relief valve (right); The flow control; The check valve. Hint on The flow control: "That sets the speed. The ram has stopped, so no oil passes it now." Hint on The check valve: "That lets oil into the rod side only. It is shut while the ram comes down." Why: the ram cannot move, so the pressure rises until the relief valve opens. Its setting is the highest the pressure can reach. So it decides how hard the ram presses. After Check, the relief path lights and the relief valve rings. Screen 8, show, Back up: the ram on the work, both solenoids off. Words: "Energise -Y2 and the crossed box joins P to B and A to T. Oil reaches the rod side through the check valve. The piston side drains to the tank, and the ram goes back up." Then "Tap -Y2, then tap it again." Read: both solenoids are off, and the ram holds part way up. Before that, -Y2 was on. Oil ran from P to B through the check valve into the rod side, and from A to T to the tank. Then -Y2 went off, and the middle box blocked A and B. Still: the ram held part way up. Screen 9, do, Into the rod side: -Y2 marked as on, the crossed box against the ports, no path lit. "-Y2 is on. Which way does most of the oil reach the rod side?" Choices: Through the check valve (right); Through the flow control; It cannot, the check valve blocks it. Hint on Through the flow control: "The check valve beside it opens this way, so most of the oil takes the easy path." Hint on It cannot: "A check valve lets flow one way. Read which way its ball lifts off the seat." Why: going into the rod side, the oil lifts the check valve's ball off its seat. So most of it passes the flow control by. The ram goes up quickly, and comes down at the flow control's speed. After Check, the path lights. Screen 10, show, The same job in air: the air card. Words: "The same job in air uses a 5/2 valve. Energise -Y3 and the supply fills the piston side. The rod side's air leaves through an exhaust port, marked as a key term, into the room. Air also squeezes. So a cylinder holding a load on shut-in air gives as the load grows." Then "Tap -Y3, then drag the load slider." Read: -Y3 is on. The supply runs into the piston side, the rod side's air leaves through an exhaust port, and the rod is out. In the squeeze test beside it, at 12 bar absolute, the air fills 150 cm³ and its rod is pushed in. The oil's rod has not moved. Still: -Y3 on, the slider at 12. Screen 11, do, Where does the air go?: the air card, -Y3 marked as on, only the supply path lit. "Where does the air from the rod side go?" Choices: Out of an exhaust port, into the room (right); Back along a line to the receiver; Back to the compressor. Hint on the receiver: "No line runs back to the receiver. Look for the exhaust marks on the valve." Hint on the compressor: "A compressor draws in fresh air from the room. Used air is not sent back to it." Why: the box -Y3 brings in joins the rod side to an exhaust port. So the used air leaves into the room. Oil is kept and used again, so the press sends it back to the tank. After Check, the exhaust path lights. Screen 12, show, Pressure stays: -Y1 on, the ram on the work. Words: "Stop stops the pump and switches both solenoids off. The springs centre the valve while the ram still presses the work. That shuts its oil in. The oil still holds the ram down, so its line turns red. Pressure shut in like this is stored energy., stored energy marked as a key term" Then "Tap Stop." Read: the pump has stopped, both solenoids are off and the gauge reads zero. The line from A is red, labelled still under pressure. The ram is still on the work. Still: the pump stopped. Screen 13, do, mixed, Safe to open?: the press as screen 12 left it, with the line from A still drawn plain. "You must change the hose to the piston side. The motor is stopped and the pump's gauge reads zero. Is the hose safe to open?" Choices: No, oil shut in by the centred valve can still be under pressure (right); Yes, the gauge reads zero; Yes, both solenoids are off. Hint on the gauge: "That gauge reads the pump's line only. The middle box blocks A, so the hose is cut off from it." Hint on the solenoids: "With both off, the middle box blocks A and B. That shuts oil in rather than letting it out." Why: the middle box blocks A. So the oil between A and the cylinder is shut in, and it still holds the ram on the work. Release that pressure and prove that part at zero before you open the hose. After Check, the line from A turns red and pulses. Screen 14, do, mixed, Top of the stroke: the press running, -Y2 marked as on, the ram right at the top. "-Y2 is still on and the ram has reached the top. Where does the pump's oil go now?" Choices: Over the relief valve to the tank (right); Into the rod side through the check valve; Through the middle box, from P to T. Hint on Into the rod side: "The ram can rise no further, so no more oil can get in." Hint on the middle box: "-Y2 is still on, so the crossed box is against the ports, not the middle one." Why: at the end of its travel, no more oil can enter the rod side. The pressure climbs until the relief valve opens. Then the pump's oil goes over it to the tank. Switch -Y2 off and the P to T centre unloads the pump. After Check, the relief path lights.
interactive.ignores: Time is sped up. Every line is drawn with no pressure drop along it. The pump's oil is drawn splitting in fixed shares between the cylinder and the relief valve. In a real fixed pump, that split shifts as the load changes. The squeeze test shuts the air in. This 5/2 valve cannot do that, because neither of its boxes blocks both cylinder lines. Real oil squeezes a very little, so even trapped oil gives slightly. Shut-in pressure is drawn as staying. In a real circuit it falls slowly as oil leaks past the spool, sometimes over hours. The gauge has no scale. This lesson does not show how big the parts must be or how fast the ram goes. The ram's speed depends on the pump's flow and the cylinder's size.

explain.text:
To read a fluid power circuit, take one valve position at a time and trace two paths. One runs from the supply to one side of the cylinder. The other runs from the cylinder's other side back to the tank. In air, it runs out through an exhaust instead. The side that is fed and the side that is emptied tell you which way the cylinder moves.

Start with the job, then the parts. This press brings a ram down onto the work, squeezes it and lifts it again. A motor drives a pump. The pump draws oil from the tank through a filter. A relief valve and a gauge sit on the pump's line. A 4/3 valve with solenoids -Y1 and -Y2 steers the oil to the cylinder. The solenoids are coils. So the control schematic draws what energises them, and you find them there by the same tags. On the line to the rod side, a flow control sits beside a check valve.

Next read the drawn state. The sheet shows each part in its normal, or neutral, condition.[^1] Here the springs hold the valve's middle box against the ports. That box joins P to T and blocks A and B. So the pump's oil goes back to the tank at low pressure, and the ram holds.

Now energise -Y1. The left box joins P to A, so the pump's oil fills the piston side. It also joins B to T. While one side is fed, the other is lined up to drain back to the tank. That second path matters as much as the first. Oil barely squeezes. So the ram comes down only as fast as the rod side's oil gets out. That oil must pass the flow control. The check valve beside it opens only for oil going into the rod side. So the flow control sets the ram's speed.

A fixed pump pushes out the same amount of oil every turn. That is more than the flow control lets through. So the pressure rises until the relief valve opens and takes the rest. Once the ram stops on the work, the relief valve takes it all. Its setting decides how hard the ram presses.

Energise -Y2 instead and the crossed box joins P to B and A to T. Oil reaches the rod side through the check valve, and the ram goes back up. The route the oil takes in one valve position is its [[flow path]].

The same job in air uses a 5/2 valve. Energise its solenoid and the supply reaches the piston side. The rod side is exhausted, and the rod comes out. The used air leaves through an [[exhaust port]] on the valve, into the room. It never comes back. Air also squeezes. So a cylinder holding a load on shut-in air gives as the load grows.

Last, stopping the pump does not empty the circuit. Oil shut in by a centred valve can still hold the ram on the work. Pressure shut in like this is [[stored energy]]. It must be released before anyone opens a line.

**For each valve position, trace the supply to one side of the cylinder and the other side out to the tank or exhaust. The side fed and the side emptied together decide what moves.**

analogy.text: You know this from tracing a single-phase load. You follow the line out to it and the neutral back. Find only the line and you have not found the circuit. No current flows without the way back. A cylinder is the same. One side is fed and the other must be emptied. An oil cylinder whose way out is shut barely moves.
analogy.breaks: A neutral carries back the same current the line takes out. A cylinder's two sides take different amounts of oil, because the rod fills part of the rod side. In air there is no way back at all. The used air leaves through the exhaust.

practice.text:
- Safety first. A stopped pump does not mean a dead circuit. Oil shut in by a centred valve stays under pressure. So does oil holding up a raised load. Lower or prop the load and isolate the pump. Then release the pressure by the plant's procedure. Prove the part you will open reads zero, not just the pump's gauge.
- Read the job. What is the circuit for, and what moves?
- Name the parts. Find the supply, and the tank or the exhausts.
- Read the drawn state. Find which box sits against the ports with nothing operating the valve.
- For each position, slide its box in. Trace the supply to one side of the cylinder, then the other side out to the tank or exhaust. Say what moves and which way.
- For each position, find what sets the speed, what limits the pressure and what holds the load.
- Find the solenoids on the control schematic by their tags. That shows what energises them.

**Rule of thumb:** every position has two paths, one in and one out. If you cannot find the way out, an oil cylinder will barely move.

**Worked example:** the press. As drawn, the middle box joins P to T, so the pump unloads and the ram holds. With -Y1 on, oil goes from P to A into the piston side. The rod side's oil goes through the flow control and B to T, to the tank. The ram comes down at the flow control's speed. On the work it stops. The relief valve sets how hard it presses. With -Y2 on, oil goes from P to B through the check valve into the rod side. The piston side drains from A to T, and the ram goes up quickly.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the drawn position as the working one.
- Following only the fed side and missing the way out.
- Expecting a check valve to pass oil both ways.
- Looking for a return line on an air circuit.
- Trusting the pump's gauge to say the whole circuit is at zero.

sources.quote: Each symbol is drawn to show the normal or neutral condition of each component unless multiple circuit diagrams are furnished showing various phases of circuit operation
